newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says it may seek UN observer status.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says it may seek UN observer status.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister said on Thursday his island would continue its quest to join the United Nations, despite China's objections, but conceded Taipei may have to settle initially for U.N. observer status.

Speaking before leaving on a diplomatic mission to Guatemala, Foreign Minister John Chang told reporters that Taiwan may seek observer membership before trying again for full entry into the United Nations.
"We may try to go the route of observer member. We do not rule out such thinking," Chang said.
Taiwan's arch rival China and its supporters blocked moves in the U.N. General Assembly in September to consider membership for Taiwan, scuttling Taipei's bid for a fourth straight year.

Chang said his ministry would study input from the National Development Conference, a state-sponsored multiparty forum on national affairs under way in Taipei, before devising strategies for seeking observer membership.
"Whatever consensus that comes out of the conference will be an important reference for us," Chang said.
The ad hoc conference concludes on December 28.
China, which has veto power in the U.N. Security Council, regards Taiwan as a renegade province and deems any bid to give Taiwan membership an intolerable breach of its sovereignty.

Taiwan's Republic of China government lost China's U.N. seat to Beijing in 1971, more than two decades after it fled to the island in 1949 when it lost the civil war with the communists on the Chinese mainland.
China's efforts to keep Taiwan out of the U.N. are part of a diplomatic squeeze that Beijing has been tightening in hopes of bringing Taiwan under its rule.
China won a major victory in November when South Africa, the largest of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies, announced it would switch recognition to Beijing in 1997.
Taipei has been sending top officials abroad on diplomatic missions, including Chang's upcoming Guatemala trip, in the hope of preventing further desertions to Beijing.
